final_proof:
Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra over a set $X$.
By definition, $\Sigma$ is closed under countable unions, which implies it is also closed under finite unions. Thus, for any $A, B \in \Sigma$, their union $A \cup B$ is in $\Sigma$.
Therefore, the set union operation $\cup$ is a closed binary operation on $\Sigma$.
A magma of sets is a collection of sets equipped with a closed binary set operation. Since $\Sigma$ is equipped with the closed binary operation of set union, the structure $(\Sigma, \cup)$ is a magma.
Consequently, the concept of a $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets.
